quote: Wenn man irgend ein System von Axiomen hat, so kann man fragen, ob [-das-] {+mein+} Vollständigkeitsaxiom überhaupt hinzuzufügen möglich ist d.h. ob es nicht widerspre- chend [?] [-ist-] sei bez. welche Axiome noch vorher hinzugefügt werden müssen, damit [-d-]
english: If one has any system of axioms, one can ask whether it is possible at all to add my completeness axiom, i.e. whether it is not contradictory, or which axioms must first be added so that [sentence continues on next page].
topic: Reflections on the axiomatic method: that it unifies branches internally, that old theories reappear in new ones, that it frees the scholar from chance and is a 'democratic' method, and the question of whether a completeness axiom can be added to a system of axioms.

triage.modern_statement: Take an axiom system T and add Hilbert's completeness axiom, which is a maximality or non-extensibility condition: 'no model of T can be properly extended to a larger structure that still satisfies T.' Two questions follow. (a) When is T together with this maximality axiom consistent, meaning T has a maximal model with respect to the substructure or extension relation? (b) If it is not consistent, which extra axioms must be added to T first? The standard case is the reals. Every ordered field has a proper ordered-field extension, so the maximality axiom contradicts the ordered-field axioms on their own. Once the Archimedean axiom is added, it becomes consistent: R is the unique maximal Archimedean ordered field. Hilbert's Euclidean geometry, where the Archimedean axiom also comes first, works the same way. The general version of the question, about 'extremal axioms' for arbitrary axiom systems, is a metatheoretical question that was later studied explicitly.
triage.answered_by: For the cases Hilbert cared about (arithmetic and geometry), Hilbert himself answered it in print. The completeness axiom appeared in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1900), the French edition of the Grundlagen (1900) and the 2nd German edition (1903). He stated it relative to the Archimedean axiom and noted that it can only be satisfied if the Archimedean axiom holds. In the 7th edition (1930) it was reformulated as the 'linear completeness' axiom. The question was then studied explicitly by Richard Baldus, 'Zur Axiomatik der Geometrie I: Über Hilberts Vollständigkeitsaxiom', Math. Ann. 100 (1928), 321–333. Carnap and Bachmann (1936) later treated general 'extremal axioms'. I could not open these papers' contents in my search, so their exact theorems are not confirmed here.

evidence.claim: Baldus published a paper devoted specifically to Hilbert's completeness axiom: 'Zur Axiomatik der Geometrie I. Über Hilberts Vollständigkeitsaxiom', Mathematische Annalen 100, 321–333 (1928), received 27 Sept 1927.

Using the completeness axiom to characterize R and Euclidean space depends on also assuming the Archimedean axiom, and Hilbert acknowledged this himself. The arithmetical completeness axiom says R has no proper extension to an Archimedean ordered field.
The literature compares Baldus (1928), who followed Hilbert's line, with Carnap and Bachmann (1936) on completeness axioms and, more generally, extremal (maximal) axioms in Hilbert's Grundlagen.
Carnap's work on extremality axioms cites Baldus 1928 and also Baldus 1938, 'Über nicht beweisbare und doch entbehrliche Axiome', Math. Z. 44.
The completeness axiom was added in the French 1st edition (1900) and the 2nd German edition (1903). Linear completeness came in the 7th edition (1930).
Historical work on Hilbert's metatheory connects his consistency problem to the role of the completeness axiom in both geometrical and arithmetical axiom systems.

triage.why: The note asks a recognizable metatheoretical question: when can Hilbert's maximality-type completeness axiom be added consistently to an axiom system, and which axioms (in practice, the Archimedean axiom) must come first? For the systems Hilbert was working on, this was settled in his own published work. The Archimedean axiom makes the completeness axiom satisfiable, by R and the Cartesian model. Baldus (1928) then analysed the question in a dedicated paper, and Carnap and Bachmann (1936) generalized it to extremal axioms. It is not one of the 23 Paris problems and is not usually called an open problem. The mathematical part counts as answered. Work continues mainly in history and philosophy of mathematics (e.g. Giovannini; Bonatti, Erkenntnis 2026), not as an open research problem in mathematics. Confidence is medium for two reasons: I could not read the full texts of Baldus or Carnap–Bachmann to confirm their exact theorems, and the diary sentence breaks off mid-sentence, so its exact scope (geometry only, or arbitrary axiom systems) is somewhat uncertain.
